analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal land to oil, gas, and oil shale leasing while shortening environmental reviews and limiting lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 228-192 on November 20, 2013, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would speed up oil and gas drilling permits on federal land — approving them automatically if the Interior Department doesn't decide within 60 days — and require at least a quarter of newly nominated federal acreage to be leased each year with limited chance to object. It would lock in Bush-era oil shale rules as legally final, mandate oil shale lease sales in Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming, and force annual leasing in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. It would also make it harder and costlier for citizens to challenge energy projects in court, capping injunctions at 60 days, presuming agency decisions correct, and blocking recovery of attorneys' fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies get faster, near-automatic drilling permits and leases that can't be cancelled after purchase or burdened with new conditions. Oil shale developers get legally protected leasing rules and mandated commercial lease sales for a fuel that has never been produced commercially at scale. Companies also benefit from shorter court challenges and no attorney-fee risk from opponents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and oil shale developers

how_it_helps.text: A drilling permit application is deemed approved if Interior does not decide within 60 days of receiving it.

Interior must offer at least 25% of annually nominated federal acreage for lease each year, shielded from protest and from the 'extraordinary circumstances' environmental test, and eligible for expedited environmental review.
Interior may not cancel a lease parcel after a competitive sale, may not add lease conditions after sale without the company's agreement, and may not indefinitely delay project approvals or permits.

The 2008 federal oil shale regulations and land-use decisions are deemed to satisfy every legal requirement, including the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, and Interior must hold at least five commercial oil shale lease sales of at least 25,000 acres each by January 1, 2016.

Courts must presume agency findings correct in challenges to energy projects, preliminary injunctions halting projects are limited to 60 days at a time, and challengers cannot recover attorneys' fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act.
Annual lease sales are mandated in the most oil-rich parts of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska through 2023, with permits for roads and pipelines required on set timelines.

analysis.who_pays: Communities and taxpayers near drilling on public land bear the environmental and water-quality risk of shortened review, and a $5,000 fee makes objecting to a lease sale expensive for ordinary groups. Public land users lose access protections, and citizens lose their most practical legal tools — injunctions and fee recovery — when an agency approves a project unlawfully. Taxpayers also fund up to $50 million in state oil and gas resource assessments and underwrite oil shale leasing rules written before commercial feasibility was demonstrated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public-land users, rural communities, and litigants

drawbacks.text: A $5,000 documentation fee would be charged for every protest of a federal lease, right-of-way, or drilling permit — a barrier for conservation groups, local governments, and individuals objecting to a sale.

The bill rewrites judicial review for energy projects: administrative findings are presumed correct, injunctions are limited to 60-day windows, challengers face strict standing and 90-day filing deadlines, and no attorney's fees can be awarded — stacking the process toward the agency and industry.

The oil shale provisions declare 2008 regulations and land-use plans legally sufficient under every environmental law, insulating them from challenge, and mandate five commercial lease sales by 2016 even though commercial oil shale production has never been demonstrated in the United States.
A Democratic motion to recommit — which would have protected Native American sacred and cultural sites from required energy development — was rejected 189-232, on a nearly pure party-line vote.

Interior's proposed hydraulic fracturing rules would have no force on Indian trust lands without beneficiary consent, and environmental reviews of projects on Indian land could be commented on only by tribe members and area residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill carries a few narrower benefits — internet-based lease auctions intended to raise more money for taxpayers, and tribal provisions giving tribes more control over appraisals, long-term leasing, and biomass projects. But its core effect is to shift federal land energy policy toward faster leasing with fewer checks: shorter environmental review, harder and costlier public objection, and court rules tilted against challengers. The costs to environmental protection, community objection rights, and the Treasury (through fee-financed permitting and underwritten oil shale leasing) outweigh those narrower gains.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line 228-192 vote in November 2013, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on a 27-14 vote on July 24, 2013, and reported it amended on November 12, 2013.

The House Rules Committee structured floor debate to allow only a limited set of amendments, and the House passed the bill 228-192 on November 20, 2013, with Republicans voting 221-1 for it and Democrats 7-191 against.
A motion to recommit with instructions to protect Native American sacred and cultural sites failed 189-232, with 224 of 230 voting Republicans opposed.
The Senate received the bill on November 21, 2013, read it twice, and placed it on the calendar on December 9, 2013; no vote ever occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people and public-land protections came out ahead: the expanded leasing, shortened environmental review, protest fees, and court restrictions never became law. Oil and gas companies did not gain the automatic-permit and lease-protection provisions they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public lands and the people who use them

for.name: Rep. Doug Lamborn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House.

for.name: House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill, ordered it reported 27-14, and reported it amended on November 12, 2013.

for.name: House Rules Committee and Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Structured the rule for H.R. 1965 and companion H.R. 2728, allowing only pre-printed amendments and one motion to recommit.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a Senate vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in December 2013.

against.name: Rep. Ann Kirkpatrick
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit with instructions to protect Native American sacred and cultural sites from required energy development; failed 189-232.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration publicly opposed the bill and urged its rejection, consistent with the veto threats it issued for the related federal-lands energy bills considered the same week.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party: 221 of 230 Republicans voted yes versus 7 of 200 Democrats, and the failed motion to recommit split the other way, 224 Republicans against to 188 Democrats for.

industries.note: Drilling permits would be approved automatically if Interior misses a 60-day deadline, at least a quarter of newly nominated acreage must be offered annually with protest largely blocked, and leases could not be cancelled after purchase. Shortened environmental review and limited court challenges shift drilling's air, water, and land risks onto nearby communities and the public.

industries.industry: Oil shale and tar sands developers
industries.note: The bill declares 2008 oil shale rules and land plans legally final under every environmental law and mandates five commercial lease sales of at least 25,000 acres by 2016, despite commercial oil shale production never having been demonstrated in the U.S. This hands leasing certainty to a speculative industry before its economics or environmental footprint are proven.

industries.industry: Wind and solar developers on federal land
industries.note: Right-of-way fee collections are redirected to fund solar and wind permitting at Interior, capped at $5 million a year. This modestly speeds renewable permitting but the bill's overall design favors oil, gas, and oil shale.

A $5,000 fee per protest, strict filing deadlines and standing rules, 60-day injunction limits, and a ban on attorney-fee recovery sharply reduce these groups' ability to challenge leasing decisions, which is the main check on how public land is developed.

Tribes gain faster appraisal decisions, 99-year Navajo commercial leasing, and biomass demonstration projects — real tools for economic development. But the bill also bars federal fracking rules on trust land without consent and limits who can comment on environmental reviews of projects on Indian land.
